title: When not to use deep learning: tabular data, little data, and the boosting baseline

videos.script: This course has trained networks for nineteen lessons. This one asks when not to. {{question}} Most of the data a company holds is a table. One row per case, one column per measurement. {{table}} On a table of tumour measurements, three models finish within about one point. {{cancer}} Logistic regression wins. The network comes last, and it takes the longest. {{clock}} On a table of customers, shaped by rules with thresholds, boosting wins outright. {{churn}} A tree cuts at a threshold exactly. A network has to bend towards it. {{step}} Then the digits again, with two images of each, then five, then twenty. {{small}} With twenty images, the convolutional network is last. With all of them, it is first. {{cross}} So the lesson gives a recipe. Run gradient boosting with its defaults before any network. {{recipe}} It even takes missing values that logistic regression refuses. {{refused}} And then the other side. Move each digit one pixel, and boosting falls apart. {{moved}} The convolutional network keeps most of its accuracy, because it learnt its own features. {{features}} That is what deep learning is for: images, sound and text. {{media}} The lesson ends with a checklist, and the course ends with it. {{end}}
